film.credit: Sound on; captions in the player menu
p1: At twenty to three on Thursday 5 November three people left Tesa 41 with the Italian flag on their backs: one green unit, one white, one red, each strapped to a frame. They walked to San Francesco della Vigna, on to the great campo of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, Zanipolo to Venetians, then to Santa Maria Formosa, and home another way. About two and a half kilometres, an hour and a quarter. It was the first of the walks.
fig.vigna-campo: Setting out: three units across a campo in Castello
p2: Two weeks earlier, on 22 October, a single red unit had gone out the same door on Aram Zadikian’s back. We wrote about that afternoon in Carrying. It was a test: of the frame, of the straps, of the wind on the quay, and of what Venice would make of it. Even then the talk on the way was of more. “At least six,” Aram said. Zadik agreed.
p3: Three is the smallest number that makes a flag. One red unit on a back is a form in the street; green, white and red walking side by side is something everybody recognises before they have really looked. The flag the studio built in Tesa 41 stands on its own feet. On 5 November it walked on other people’s.
p4: Those people were students of the Accademia di Belle Arti di Venezia, the city’s academy of fine arts. When a passer-by asked who was carrying, Zadik pointed: “They’re over there, the students. They’re helping me, from the Venice Academy of Arts.”
fig.church-front: Set down before a church door
p5: The route went by the wide ways, rive, fondamente and campi, where three tall forms can pass and be set down without blocking anyone. At each stop the carriers stood in a row, and the city did what cities do: it looked.
p6: The film keeps some of what was said. Introducing the work to people in a campo: “This is the Armenian Pavilion, and the Armenian artist is right here, and he created a tribute to the country of Italy, which is their flag.” Someone answered: “Thank you for the tribute.” And, a moment later: “Thank you for what your people have been doing through history, because that’s very important.”
fig.zanipolo-colleoni: In Campo Santi Giovanni e Paolo, under Verrocchio’s Colleoni
fig.zanipolo-wide: Campo Santi Giovanni e Paolo, before the Scuola Grande di San Marco
p7: Another passer-by found the words we had been looking for: “It’s a travelling flag.” Zadik: “It’s a journey. We are taking a journey in Venice.”
p8: And heads turned, all afternoon. “We are turning people’s heads around,” Zadik said. “Anytime they see it, they’re just looking: what the hell is this?” And later, sitting down: “We’re sitting in this historic square. We’re making history again.”
h2.plan: The plan: out and back, every few days
p9: The walks go on until the Biennale closes. Each one leaves Tesa 41 by the door on the Fondamenta Case Nuove, follows a different route out, sets the works down in two or three places, and comes home another way. The number of works grows: three on the first day, six on the next walk, then twelve. On 18 November students of the Accademia walk them to the Accademia itself, one work on each student’s back, into its cloister at 11:00, for an hour with its professors and students. The last walk is on the closing day.
p10: This is the plan as it stood on 5 November. Routes and times may still move: the up-to-date schedule, the map of every route and the photographs of each walk are on the Walks page. Anyone may walk alongside: meet at the door of Tesa 41 ten minutes before the time.
p11: The weight is not only in the units. It is in the carrying: in kilometres of stone underfoot, in being looked at, and in carrying another country’s colours through its own city, as guests. One unit was a test. Three is a flag. Twelve, we hope, will be something else again.
p12: The next walk leaves Tesa 41 tomorrow, with six. Come and walk with us.
